title: Computational versus statistical privacy in the curator model
formal: Historical question: can computational assumptions permit greater utility in the trusted-curator model when differential privacy is required only against polynomial-time adversaries? The intended separation compares an efficient computationally private mechanism with all statistically private mechanisms, including computationally unbounded ones. In precise asymptotic form, a separating theorem provides a family of polynomial-time binary utility tests \((u_\kappa)\), one efficient mechanism family with a fixed constant computational-privacy parameter and utility \(1-o(1)\), and an impossibility result for every constant-privacy statistical mechanism family with negligible additive slack and any positive constant worst-case utility. The source expressly invites computational assumptions; it does not demand unconditional existence of cryptographic primitives. This is a historical question now conditionally resolved by FOCS 2023 Theorem 5 under its three explicitly named assumptions. It is archived with that qualification, rather than replaced by a new unconditional separation conjecture.
why: This asks whether the information released under privacy can become more useful merely by restricting the adversary’s computational power, even when a single curator already holds all records. It distinguishes a change in achievable accuracy from a faster implementation and from the benefits of distributing trust. A separation changes the theoretical interpretation of statistical privacy lower bounds.
status_note: Conditionally resolved in the source’s invited computational-assumption sense by FOCS 2023 Theorem 5, under its Assumptions 18, 22 and 26. The result separates achievable utility even against unbounded statistical curators. No assertion is made that these assumptions have been proved or that the archived shorthand fully defines a new Lean target. The original paragraph, theorem, privacy definitions and assumption list were checked on 15 September 2026.

importance.reason: A central foundational comparison between computational and statistical privacy, with implications for whether privacy lower bounds survive cryptographic restrictions. The strong published conditional utility separation resolves the historical broad question in its invited assumption-based sense, while leaving practical and weaker-assumption variants distinct.

sentences: The historical question asks whether computational assumptions can improve utility for one trusted private-data curator.
Computational privacy protects against efficient tests, whereas statistical privacy protects against every test.
A FOCS 2023 theorem conditionally separates these notions in utility even when the statistical curator has unlimited computation.
Its conclusion depends on keyless hashing, a specified differing-inputs obfuscation assumption, and non-interactive witness-indistinguishable proofs.
The question is archived as conditionally resolved, with those assumptions preserved and without claiming an unconditional separation or a new formalized benchmark.

definitions: A trusted curator receives the entire private dataset and produces one public output. A security parameter \(\kappa\in\mathbb N\) controls the lengths of records and outputs, each polynomial in \(\kappa\); the dataset has polynomially many records. A mechanism family is efficient if one randomized algorithm computes it in time polynomial in \(\kappa\) and the input length. A binary utility test \(u_\kappa(D,y)\) is uniformly polynomial-time computable; utility at least \(\alpha_\kappa\) means \(\Pr[u_\kappa(D,M_\kappa(D))=1]\ge\alpha_\kappa\) for every allowed dataset, not only a random dataset. A nonnegative function \(\nu\) is negligible if for every integer \(a>0\), eventually \(\nu(\kappa)\le\kappa^{-a}\). Statistical \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-privacy requires \(\Pr[M(D)\in E]\le e^{\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D')\in E]+\delta\) for all adjacent datasets and all output events. Indistinguishability-based computational privacy instead requires the analogous inequality for each polynomial-size adversarial test circuit applied to the output, with negligible additive slack, uniformly over polynomial-length sequences of adjacent datasets; its randomness includes the mechanism and the test. This is IND-CDP, rather than the stronger requirement of being indistinguishable from an actual statistically private mechanism. The FOCS result uses insertion/deletion of one record as adjacency; replacing a record is covered by two such steps and changes constant privacy parameters only by constant factors. The three hypotheses of the historical resolution are non-interactive witness-indistinguishable proofs (Assumption 26), laconic collision-resistant keyless hash functions (Assumption 18), and differing-inputs obfuscation for public-coin samplers with the particular sampler security requirement in Assumption 22. These names identify exact external security assumptions of the cited theorem; their full security games are not redefined or asserted true here. This archival record does not certify a new self-contained Lean benchmark conditional on abbreviated predicates.
answer_criterion: The historical question is answered by a mathematically proved conditional separation under explicitly stated computational assumptions, provided the utility is efficiently testable and the statistical impossibility includes unbounded curators. A Lean version would have to formalize the full selected assumptions and prove both the computational-privacy utility guarantee and the matching statistical impossibility from them; naming the assumptions is not itself such a formalization. An efficiency separation alone, a multiparty separation, or a simulation-based notion with a matching statistical simulator does not establish this utility separation. The archived conditional theorem is not an unconditional proof that its cryptographic assumptions hold.

source_formulation.text: Can computational assumptions improve what a trusted curator can achieve under differential privacy?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: The textbook first describes how cryptography improves distributed private aggregation by allowing separated participants to simulate a trusted curator. It then asks whether computational assumptions also help when that curator is already present. This latter question concerns achievable utility and is not answered merely by the distributed simulation.

Bun, Chen and Vadhan obtained a conditional central-model separation involving efficient statistically private mechanisms in 2016. Their task still has an inefficient statistical mechanism with matching parameters. That distinguishes computation costs, but does not demonstrate utility impossible under statistical privacy itself. The FOCS 2023 introduction explicitly distinguishes these targets.

FOCS 2023 Theorem 5 provides polynomial-time utility tests and, for any constant \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{CDP}}>0\), an efficient IND-CDP mechanism with worst-case utility \(1-o(1)\). Under Assumptions 18, 22 and 26, it also rules out every statistically \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SDP}},\kappa^{-27})\)-private mechanism with positive constant utility, for any constant \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{SDP}}>0\). The latter quantifier includes computationally unbounded curators. Impossibility at \(\kappa^{-27}\) also covers negligible additive slack for sufficiently large security parameters.

All three computational assumptions are conditions of the result. The publication does not prove the existence of the assumed keyless hashing, obfuscation and witness-indistinguishable proof systems. The utility task is specifically constructed for the separation and produces a circuit accompanied by a verifiable object; the theorem does not assert improved accuracy for every ordinary statistical query. These limits do not remove its role as an affirmative conditional answer to the broad historical question.

Later work distinguishes computational privacy definitions for larger privacy parameters and non-negligible additive slack. In particular, an IND-CDP versus simulation-variant separation is a different comparison from the central computational-versus-statistical utility separation here. The archived result keeps the fixed-constant parameter regime and its exact assumption list.
